title: Ex-Students Of Erstwhile Savoy College Plan Reunion June 9-10
text:
IN MEMORY OF A TEACHER

Ex-Students Of Erstwhile Savoy College Plan Reunion June 9-10

By Elizabeth Large

SAVOY — The 14th annual Savoy College reunion is scheduled for Savoy June 9 and 10 among members of the college, which came to fiery death during the summer of 1890, and still living and no more than 50 of the school's survivors are expected here for the reunion.

The reunion, started in 1937 with Savoy's J. May and Prof. Ed A. McMahon as ringleaders, is the result of the desire of former students to bind a closer relationship with old school ties.

The college was founded in 1876 by Professor Robert R. Halsell. During its first four years it was conducted by Prof. Halsell as a school for the children in Savoy and neighboring settlements.

However, in 1880 Prof. Halsell's reputation as a teacher of English literature and mathematics had spread over all of North Texas and he was able to enlarge his facilities.

As a result, on Jan. 22, 1880, a charter was granted to R. H. Halsell, Lewis Holland, J. T. Chenoweth, James Glasscock and Gus L. German to operate the Savoy Male and Female College.

The charter read that the purpose of the school was "to maintain and support an institution of learning for the education of males and females and to empower the faculty to confer the degrees of bachelor of arts, grant diplomas, certificates of proficiency and awards of merit."

From the first, the college prospered.

EXCELLENT LIBRARY

"Not only the people of Savoy and surrounding country enjoyed the services of its excellent teachers," wrote an early day historian, "but people came from far and wide over Texas and Indian Territory to seek knowledge within its walls. It has the complete first library of any school in Texas except the state university at Austin."

Many of the early day Savoy College students were larger boys and girls. Since there was no dormitories, students—and the Indians included—boarded with farm families in the town.

The private school concept lived prominently between the school's founders themselves usually lacked the foresight in administering schools. Being a new state, many locations were selected unwisely having the institution to a central location and in many cases several schools were located in the same town at the same time. In effect, many of the schools were inadequately endowed and public funds were too meager and in many instances the lack of dormitories was creating overcrowded classrooms and forcing many children back home to help with chores when they were needed.

COULDN'T START ANEW

At the insistence of the citizens of Savoy, in 1892 he returned with L. C. Gee, who later went to Wesley College, in an attempt to reopen the school. For two years classes were held in the schoolhouse manner, but efforts to raise funds to rebuild the college failed.

After the end of that time, Prof. Halsell went to Anson and taught two years and then spent years in Noble, Okla., before going to Durant.

For several years he taught at the public schools in Durant. He served in the state legislature of Oklahoma from 1912 to 1914 and later was appointed by Gov. J. B. A. Robertson as inspector of institutions for a four-year term.

He retired after this because of ill health and died as the result of a heart attack in 1924.

Prof. Halsell left in Savoy a school tie that exists in few schools today. It was memory of the aim as much as of old Savoy College that prompted the organization of the Savoy College Ex-Students in 1937.

Mrs. Jessie Gorrell Young recalled her last talk with the professor. She said he was despondent over the death of the college and it was almost impossible to cheer him up.

"You have had power as a teacher," he shouted, pacing the floor and tossing back his shaggy locks with his hands. "Will you go further with me? I used to be able to put enough thought into my students in 10 minutes to last a month. Now, I can talk my head off and not strike a spark of enthusiasm in the entire school!"

PASSING OF AN ERA

Mrs. Young said she answered him that "you didn't used to talk this way to us. You boosted us and the school went on in high gear; on a forced march, 'there shall be no Alpe'."

"I know," replied the professor, "But I'll tell you what is the matter. It's this confounded sentimentalism in the pupils! Why little 12-year-old girls write love notes to the boys! Their minds are just not on their lessons."

The professors life went on from Savoy to even greater heights in the education field in Oklahoma. And the former students have been closer together by the monthly publication of "Savoy College Ex-Reunion News." This is a small publication financed by contributions from subscribers with Mrs. J. B. Young as editor and Gus Thomasson, Benton Maxey and Fred Reynolds as associate editors.
